title: Draw the transition state
asks: Sketch the transition state of a step, with partial bonds and charges, and compare two transition states.

know.h: A transition state is the highest-energy point of one step: bonds are partly made and partly broken. It cannot be isolated. It is drawn in square brackets with a double dagger, [ ]‡.
A transition state is a peak on the energy diagram. An intermediate (such as a carbocation) is a valley: it has full bonds and a real, if short, lifetime.

How to draw one: a dotted line for every bond that is forming or breaking in that step, and a partial charge (δ+ or δ-) on every atom whose charge is changing. The partial charges add up to the total charge of the starting materials.

{{SN2}}: [Nu···C···LG]‡. The nucleophile and the leaving group are on opposite sides of the carbon, 180° apart. The three other groups lie in one plane, one drawn up, one on a wedge and one on a dash. The carbon has five groups around it.

Charges in an {{SN2}} transition state follow the charges of the reactants. Anion and neutral substrate: δ- on the nucleophile and δ- on the leaving group. Neutral amine and alkyl halide: δ+ on N and δ- on the halogen. Hydroxide and a sulfonium ion: δ- on O and δ+ on S.

{{E2}}: [HO···H···C···C···Br]‡. Four partial bonds: base to H forming, H to C breaking, the C=C π bond forming, C to leaving group breaking. δ- on the base and on the leaving group. The H and the leaving group are anti-periplanar.
{{SN1}} ionization: [{{R3C}}δ+···LGδ-]‡. Only the C-LG bond is stretched. The nucleophile is not in it, which is why rate = k[substrate].
The transition state contains whatever is in the rate law. {{SN2}} and {{E2}}: both the substrate and the nucleophile or base. {{SN1}} and {{E1}}: the substrate alone.

Hammond's postulate: a transition state looks like the species it is closest to in energy. In an exothermic step it comes early and resembles the starting materials. In an endothermic step it comes late and resembles the products of that step.
Ionization to a carbocation is endothermic, so its transition state resembles the carbocation. Whatever stabilizes the carbocation stabilizes that transition state: tertiary > secondary for {{SN1}}.

The lecture homework. A: {{I-}} with {{CH3I}}, the same group enters and leaves, so the transition state is symmetric. B: {{HO-}} with {{CH3I}}, exothermic, so the transition state is early. C: {{(CH3)3CO-}} with {{CH3I}}, the bulky nucleophile crowds the five-coordinate carbon, so the transition state is higher in energy.
Crowding raises the energy of the {{SN2}} transition state, because five groups surround one carbon. That is the reason for methyl > primary > secondary >>> tertiary.

method: Write the step with its curved arrows, so you know which bonds form and which break.
Draw the atoms in the geometry of the step: backside attack for SN2, H and leaving group anti for E2, a stretched C-LG bond for ionization.
Draw every forming or breaking bond as a dotted line and leave the other bonds solid.
Put δ+ or δ- on each atom whose charge changes, and check that the total equals the charge of the starting materials.
Close the brackets and add the double dagger.
For Hammond's postulate, decide whether the step is exothermic or endothermic, then say which side the transition state resembles.

pitfalls.h: Drawing full bonds and full charges. That is an intermediate or a product, not a transition state.
Putting the nucleophile and the leaving group on the same side of the carbon in {{SN2}}.
Putting the nucleophile in the transition state of the {{SN1}} ionization.
Leaving out the partial C=C bond or the base in the {{E2}} transition state.
Using Hammond's postulate backwards: an exothermic step has a transition state like its starting materials, not like its products.
Forgetting the brackets and the double dagger.
